title: The Personal Computer — From Altair to Apple to IBM PC

panels.text: In January 1975, the MITS Altair 8800 — a kit computer based on the Intel 8080, sold for $439 — had no keyboard, no screen, and was programmed by flipping toggle switches. It was, by any practical measure, nearly useless. It changed everything.

panels.prompt: Two young men in their late teens hunched intensely over a large PDP-10 terminal at a university computer lab in the mid-1970s, one with glasses focused on the screen, the other pointing excitedly at code, pizza boxes and soda cans nearby, fluorescent lighting, vintage 1970s college atmosphere, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, purple accent on terminal glow 1970s computing aesthetic only — green phosphor CRT terminal, NO modern flat screens, NO laptops.
panels.label: Bill Gates and Paul Allen writing Altair BASIC on a Harvard PDP-10

panels.text: Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote a BASIC interpreter for the Altair on a Harvard PDP-10, using a homemade emulator — they had never touched an Altair. When Allen demonstrated it, the software ran on real hardware for the first time. It worked. They founded Microsoft in April 1975.

In February 1976, Gates published an angry "Open Letter to Hobbyists," arguing that copying software without paying was theft: "Who can afford to do professional work for nothing?" The hobbyist community was furious — many saw software as something to be freely shared. This letter is often cited as the opening shot in the free vs. commercial software debate.

panels.label: Steve Wozniak at the Homebrew Computer Club with the Apple I circuit board

panels.text: Steve Wozniak designed the Apple I single-handedly and gave away the schematics. His friend Steve Jobs convinced him the designs could be sold. They founded Apple Computer on April 1, 1976. The Apple II (1977) — with color graphics and eventually the VisiCalc spreadsheet (1979), the first "killer app" — made personal computing real for businesses.

panels.prompt: An IBM PC from 1981 sitting on a clean office desk with a green phosphor monitor displaying a DOS prompt, a keyboard and beige system unit, a businessman in a suit looking at it with curiosity, wood-paneled office walls, the tagline A COMPUTER FOR EVERYONE visible on a poster, vintage corporate atmosphere, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, purple accent highlights
panels.label: The IBM PC, August 1981 — computing goes corporate

panels.text: On August 12, 1981, the IBM PC launched with an open architecture. Microsoft supplied MS-DOS, acquired for around $50,000–$75,000 — and crucially retained the right to sell DOS to other manufacturers. This single licensing decision would make Microsoft one of the most valuable companies on Earth.
The personal computer did not just shrink computing. It changed who could compute. Power shifted from institutions to individuals. From priests of the mainframe to anyone with a desk and a dream.

panels.text: Computers were personal now. But they were islands — each one isolated, unable to talk to any other. Quietly, in the background, a network had been growing since 1969. And its first message was an accident.
